papers.abstract: Understanding how planets and stellar companions survive and interact with their host stars as they evolve, or are ultimately destroyed in the process, is essential both for predicting the long-term future of planetary systems like our own and the contribution of stars to galactic chemical evolution. In this white paper, we discuss how the next generation ALMA (ALMA2040) will revolutionize our understanding of the key processes by detecting and characterising accreting companions and planetary engulfment signatures in hundreds of systems with evolved stars.

papers.title: From Non-Thermal to Thermal: Cosmological Imprints of Self-Interacting Secluded Dark Matter
papers.abstract: Dark matter (DM), secluded from the Standard Model (SM), can attain internal thermalization through self-interactions. We investigate the thermalization of a real scalar DM field with a quartic self-coupling, initially produced from the perturbative decay of the coherently oscillating inflaton field during reheating. The thermalization process has been studied numerically by solving Boltzmann equation of the DM momentum distribution function in presence of $2\rightarrow2$ DM elastic self-scatterings. In the absence of number-changing processes, the thermalized dark sector is characterized by a temperature and a nonzero chemical potential, determined by the inflaton mass and the reheat temperature. We find that if the inflaton mass is greater (smaller) than the reheat temperature, the DM temperature can be greater (smaller) than the SM temperature during Big Bang Nucleosynthesis, without violating any cosmological constraints. This is realized with a negative (positive) chemical potential for the DM temperature greater (smaller) than the SM one. Depending on DM production history, we can achieve the lower limit on the DM mass much below than in warm DM scenarios. The thermalization via self-scatterings tends to suppress the DM co-moving free-streaming length, compared to the non-thermal scenario without any collisions. Consequently, the lower limit on the DM mass weakens approximately by $40\%$ for a suitable choice of quartic self-coupling than in the non-thermal scenario. We obtain the lower limits on the thermal DM mass to be $2.2\times10^{-10}$ GeV and $0.47$ GeV for reheat temperatures, $5\times 10^6$ GeV and $5$ MeV respectively, while the inflaton mass is set at $10^3$ GeV.

papers.title: Hydrostatic Equilibrium Constraints on the Fuzzy Dark Matter Mass from Dwarf Spheroidals: Method, Systematics, and Robustness
papers.abstract: We present the analysis of a non-parametric estimator of the fuzzy (wave) dark matter (FDM) boson mass based on local hydrostatic equilibrium: the classical gravitational acceleration must be balanced by the gradient of the quantum potential of the Schr\"odinger-Poisson-Madelung system. We apply this condition, without assuming a soliton or any other parametric profile, to the non-parametric density and enclosed mass posteriors from pyGravSphere of the nine Milky Way dwarf spheroidal (dSph) galaxies. For each posterior realization we solve, in a least squares sense over a fixed radial window, for the boson mass that best balances the two terms, which yields a posterior distribution of mass for each galaxy. The per galaxy medians span $m\sim(0.8$-$4.6)\times10^{-20}\,\mathrm{eV}$, with Draco and Ursa Minor the lightest and Carina and Sextans the heaviest. A weighted mass estimate gives $m=(1.3\pm3.5)\times10^{-20}$ eV, dominated by Draco and Ursa Minor. We characterize the systematics in detail.

papers.title: Minkowski Functionals of CII Line Intensity Maps: Probing Astrophysics and Primordial Features
papers.abstract: Line intensity mapping aims to measure the total cumulative light of spectral lines from galaxies, without resolving individual sources. In this work, we investigate mock intensity maps of ionized carbon CII using Minkowski functionals, which capture the morphological properties of the maps. We generate semi-numerical simulations of CII intensity maps at $z\approx 6$ and $7.6$, adopting an astrophysical model that relates CII line luminosity to the mass of the host dark matter halos. We find that Minkowski functionals can provide tight constraints on the astrophysical model parameters in the presence of noise characteristics expected from the upcoming CCAT survey. We further investigate the prospects of probing a bump-like feature superimposed on the standard single power-law primordial power spectrum. Using a Fisher matrix formalism, we demonstrate that the effects of this primordial feature can be disentangled from those of the astrophysical model parameters. Combining measurements across multiple smoothing scales as well as redshifts can further improve the constraints and enhance the prospects for detecting such primordial features.

papers.title: AGN Feeding and Feedback: Resolving the Torus
papers.abstract: Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) play a key role in galaxy evolution by regulating star formation within their host galaxies. It is therefore crucial to understand how the central supermassive black holes (SMBH) are fueled by material from the galactic disk, and how AGN feedback impacts the surrounding gas. Most information so far comes from very nearby active galaxies (z < 0.008; D < 35 Mpc), providing the best spatial resolution and revealing randomly oriented dusty molecular tori that fuel SMBHs. A facility such as ALMA2040, offering significantly higher sensitivity and better angular resolution than current ALMA, would enable progress in two fundamental areas that remain beyond the capabilities of all existing and planned observatories: (i) probing the dynamics of the material feeding the AGN down to the accretion disk in nearby galaxies; and (ii) spatially resolving the tori and circum-nuclear regions of more energetic and cosmologically significant AGN, such as local quasars (z ~ 0.1 and Lbol > 10^45 erg/s).

papers.title: From Cosmic Bounces to Primordial Black Holes: The Role of Primordial Magnetic Fields
papers.abstract: We investigate primordial black hole (PBH) formation from primordial magnetic fields generated during a non-singular ekpyrotic bounce. A time-dependent coupling between the electromagnetic field and a scalar background breaks conformal invariance and amplifies gauge field fluctuations during contraction, generating magnetic fields whose anisotropic stress dominates during radiation domination. By retaining finite-wavenumber cutoffs, we compute the ultraviolet-dominated curvature spectrum, evaluate density-perturbation variance, and determine PBH abundances using both monochromatic and critical-collapse prescriptions. For benchmark parameters, the critical collapse mass spectrum peaks at $M\simeq 2.0\times10^{-3}M_\odot$ , with a total PBH dark matter fraction of $f_{PBH}\approx 10^{-5}$, forming a subdominant subsolar PBH population. Enforcing the cosmological overclosure bound ($f_{\mathrm{PBH}} \le 1$) constrains the primary background parameters, namely the end-of-contraction Hubble scale ($H_{\mathrm{end}} \le 1.6 \times 10^3~\mathrm{GeV}$) and the contraction exponent ($q \le 0.247$), establishing a physical boundary consistent with the electromagnetic backreaction limit. Shifting to asteroid-mass PBHs or a larger dark matter fraction requires modifying the ultraviolet cutoff and contraction duration. This analysis highlights the essential role of finite-wavenumber cutoffs and assumed-collapse prescriptions in linking bounce magnetogenesis to the predicted PBH abundance.

papers.title: Thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich Effect in the circumgalactic medium - III: does richness matter?
papers.abstract: We measure the thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich Effect in the circumgalactic/intragroup medium (CGM/IGrM) of 7 million $\rm M_{200c} = 10^{12-14}$M$_\odot$ $z \leqslant 1$ DESI Legacy Survey galaxies/groups using ACT+Planck observations, and investigate for the first time how the thermal pressure depends on richness. We detect the one-halo term down to 10$^{12.2}$M$_\odot$ at $5.8\sigma$. While several mass-richness bins are well described by the standard GNFW thermal-pressure profile ($\beta=5.49,r_o=0$), others favor a flatter and/or miscentered profile ($\beta=1.3-4.0,r_o>0.1 \rm R_{200c}$), with the mass dependence of this pattern varying with richness. The wide variety of thermal pressure profiles across mass and richness indicates a range of physical regimes, from dominant thermal feedback to efficient cooling with subdominant thermal feedback, and even substantial cooling. In some mass bins, the super-virial ($\approx2-7 \rm T_{200c}$) temperature floor (the lowest temperature allowed by the data for baryon-sufficient halos) points to significant heating. However, dominant kinetic-mode feedback is not essential anywhere, challenging a universal (ejective)feedback-vs-gravity picture. The slope of the thermal energy-mass relation in IGrM is consistent with self-similarity, but in the CGM it falls below self-similarity by $7.3\sigma$. This makes halos of relatively low mass and richness the dominant contributors to the universe's thermal energy budget at $z\leqslant1$. We therefore argue that calibrations of thermal energy scaling relations must move beyond the convention of using mass as the sole demarcator and instead incorporate additional intrinsic and environmental properties of galaxies.

papers.title: Probing fundamental physics with ALMA2040 mm-wavelength observations of neutron stars
papers.abstract: Bursty or (rotation-induced) pulsed coherent radio emission from pulsars, magnetars, and fast radio transients originates in some of the most extreme environments in the Universe. However, the exact physical mechanism behind the scenes remains poorly understood. ALMA2040 will allow for systematic exploration of the millimeter-wavelength spectral window for pulsars and fast radio transients for the very first time, offering unprecedented opportunities to discover new observational phenomena and advance our understanding of emission physics. Beyond this, ALMA2040 provides a unique means to unveil the neutron-star population in the Galactic Centre (GC), enable novel tests of fundamental physics in the vicinity of the supermassive black hole Sgr A*, probe the potential existence of dark matter in the GC, and investigate the dense, highly dynamic interstellar and magnetic environment of this region.

papers.title: Quantum Cosmology in Page-Wootters' Framework: Singularity Resolution and Clock Coherence
papers.abstract: We investigate the fate of big-bang singularity and coherence between distinct clock states in a quantum cosmological setting within the Page-Wootters framework. With a canonically quantized plane-symmetric Bianchi I universe, we employ Dirac factorization of the Wheeler-DeWitt constraint and obtain a Schrodinger-like equation which is first-order in an internal clock variable. By constructing its solution as a Gaussian wave packet in the expanding branch, we derive the corresponding conditional state and probability density of the universe. We find that the conditional probability density vanishes in the zero-volume limit, indicating resolution of the big-bang singularity within this probabilistic framework. Another prespective of the study is provided by the construction of density matrix from the conditional states associated with different clock readings and the remaining degree of freedom. By tracing out the remaining subsystem, we obtain the reduced density matrix and analyze the resulting coherence as a function of separation between different clock states. These results provide a relational characterization of singularity resolution and demonstrate how the spectral properties of the quantum state govern the temporal coherence between different clock states in the Page-Wootters description.

papers.title: Direct measures of black hole masses through cosmic time
papers.abstract: Supermassive black holes (BHs) are thought to reside in all massive galaxies. They play a fundamental role in shaping galaxy evolution by suppressing star formation and halting the stellar growth of the most massive galaxies via feedback mechanisms. However, to date, measuring even their most basic property, their mass, is still challenging. The mass of BHs carries information on the growth history and the mutual interplay with the host galaxy. Uncertain BH masses leave many key questions on galaxy evolution wide open. Here we show that a transformational facility such as ALMA2040 would open a new window to measure BH mass by directly observing the kinematics of cold gas in galaxy cores from the local Universe up to very high redshift, irrespective of BH activity. This would revolutionise our understanding of BH formation, growth, and their role within galaxy evolution.

papers.title: Probing cold gas and dust in quiescent galaxies across cosmic time
papers.abstract: The discovery of massive quiescent galaxies at high redshift by JWST has revealed that star formation can cease rapidly in the early Universe, yet the physical mechanisms responsible for quenching remain unknown. A key missing element is the systematic measurement in statistically representative quiescent samples of the cold gas and dust content, which are crucial for distinguishing quenching mechanisms and evolutionary pathways. Such observations are currently not feasible because state-of-the-art sub-millimeter facilities (e.g., ALMA) cannot routinely detect the faint molecular gas and dust reservoirs of quiescent galaxies, nor pinpoint outflowing molecular gas. A next-generation facility (ALMA2040) capable of providing transformative access to the cold interstellar medium of quiescent galaxies across redshift is therefore essential. In particular, it will allow the community to probe the molecular gas content of quiescent galaxies at cosmic noon and beyond by targeting the CO, [CI], and [CII] emission lines, as well as unveiling the physical conditions of the cold interstellar medium by constraining the CO spectral line energy distribution. It will also reveal the dust content of the passive population, a crucial ingredient to constrain the different quenching mechanisms. Finally, it will enable probing the molecular gas kinematics and identify molecular outflows driven by supermassive black holes. When combined with the rich legacy of JWST, ELT, and SKAO surveys, ALMA2040 will deliver a comprehensive, multi-phase view of feedback and quenching, allowing us to establish when, how, and why galaxies shut down their star formation across cosmic time.

papers.title: Dust at cosmic dawn: unveiling the onset of dust and obscured star formation at $z8$
papers.abstract: Although less than 1 percent of the baryonic mass budget of a galaxy, cosmic dust profoundly alters the multi-wavelength appearance of galaxies across cosmic time. The (sub)millimeter wavelength regime is uniquely capable of weighing these dust reservoirs, and revealing the total extent of galaxy evolution that remains hidden behind them. With current facilities, however, doing so at $z > 8$ is largely out of reach. ALMA2040, a next-generation (sub)millimeter interferometer, is set to change this. Through an order-of-magnitude increase in sensitivity compared to ALMA, ALMA2040 is a transformational facility that will be able to routinely detect dust emission from galaxies at $z > 8$ and, through simultaneous multi-band characterization, accurately measure their dust masses, temperatures, and infrared luminosities. Combined with ancillary metallicity measurements -- including from the far-infrared lines detected by ALMA2040 itself -- this will establish the relative roles of supernovae and grain growth in building up dust in the earliest galaxies. Simultaneously, ALMA2040 will measure the fraction of star formation that is obscured by dust at cosmic dawn, and thereby the extent to which rest-UV and optical surveys miss early galaxy build-up. Without a 10$\times$ upgrade to ALMA -- comparable to the leap from the VLT to the ELT -- we will not be able to capitalize on the momentous advances enabled by JWST, and will remain blind to the cold and obscured component of galaxy formation in the $z > 8$ Universe.

papers.title: Resolving the Assembly of Disk Galaxies from the Epoch of Reionisation to Cosmic Noon
papers.abstract: Most of the mass and angular momentum of today's disk galaxies assembled at $z>1$. Yet, it remains unclear how these galaxies acquired their gas, how their baryons and dark matter coevolved, and how feedback and radial gas transport shaped their disks. Addressing these gaps requires resolved observations of cold gas, which carries most of the mass and angular momentum involved in galaxy assembly. By resolving CO and [C II] at kpc scales, ALMA revealed a surprising population of rotation-dominated disks, even at $z>2$, exhibiting kinematic signatures consistent with spiral arms, bars, and tidal tails. Yet, these studies are limited to massive ($M_\star>10^{10.5}$ M$_\odot$) and highly star-forming (SFRs$\gtrsim 100$ M$_\odot$yr$^{-1}$) galaxies, the progenitors of today's most massive elliptical and disk galaxies. To understand how most present-day spirals (like the Milky Way) assembled, it is crucial to resolve their low-mass progenitors, which dominate the star-forming galaxy population by number at $z>1$. Achieving this goal demands a tenfold increase in line sensitivity and hence a next-generation sub-/millimetre facility: ALMA2040. This leap in sensitivity will enable routine resolved studies of hundreds of $M_\star>10^9$ M$_\odot$ galaxies, including those on and below the main sequence of star-forming galaxies, providing representative, statistical galaxy samples with sub-kpc constraints on the cold gas kinematics and morphology. By uniquely providing resolved CO, [C I], and [C II] observations across $z=1-6$, ALMA2040 will trace a much larger fraction of the cold-gas reservoir than is accessible today, extending resolved studies from rare massive and/or lensed systems to representative galaxy populations. In this way, ALMA2040 will transform our understanding of how galaxy disks formed and evolved.

papers.title: Model-independent parameters from DESI DR1 LRG2 with an explicitly varying power-spectrum shape
papers.abstract: Distinguishing between dark energy and modified gravity as the origin of the accelerated expansion requires the cosmic distances and the growth of structure to be measured in a model-independent way. Such measurements are difficult to perform while the primordial shape parameters are varied at the same time, and those parameters are therefore usually held fixed at the values determined by cosmic microwave background experiments. In this work, we present a methodology that constrains the shape parameters simultaneously with the model-independent distance and growth parameters, using an emulator built upon a hybrid model in which perturbative predictions are supplemented by templates measured from $N$-body simulations. {Because these templates are measured rather than expanded, the model carries non-linear corrections beyond the order at which its perturbative part is truncated, so that its accuracy on small scales is set by the simulations rather than by the reach of the expansion.} A Gaussian process emulator supplies these templates rapidly across the space of scale-dependent parameters, which makes the joint analysis computationally feasible, and the emulator is trained and validated over a range spanning $5\sigma$ of the Planck constraints. Applying the method to the LRG2 sample of DESI DR1, we obtain measurements of the Alcock--Paczynski parameters $\alpha_\perp$ and $\alpha_{||}$ and of the growth rate $f\sigma_8$. {With the tight Planck prior adopted here the constraints differ from those obtained with the shape parameters held fixed by less than a twentieth of their own uncertainties, so that the choice of template contributes at that level to the error budget of the measurement. Projected onto flat $\Lambda$CDM after the fit, the three measurements are mutually consistent, with $\chi^2=0.7$ for two degrees of freedom, and require $h=0.724\pm0.017$.

papers.title: Are High-EW LAEs good analogs for the earliest galaxies? A study on the ionizing conditions and gas properties of LAEs at $2 z7
papers.abstract: Lyman-$\alpha$ emitters (LAEs) are frequently proposed as analogs of the low-mass, metal-poor galaxies thought to dominate cosmic reionization. In particular, galaxies with large Ly$\alpha$ equivalent widths (EWs) are expected to have not experienced significant chemical enrichment. We test this hypothesis using a sample of 88 LAEs at $2 \lesssim z\lesssim 7$, selected from MUSE observations that are undetected in deep HST imaging and subsequently followed up with JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy. Despite the unprecedented sensitivity of JWST, only 50 of the LAEs exhibit secure counterparts in available deep NIRCam imaging reaching typical 3$\sigma$ depths of $m_\text{AB}\sim30.3$ mag, highlighting the intrinsically faint nature of the population. Gas-phase metallicities are inferred by fitting optical emission lines with a grid of BPASS+cloudy photoionization models, while stellar masses are derived from NIRCam photometry through SED fitting. The final sample with secure stellar masses and gas-phase metallicities encompasses only 16 LAEs, occupying regions of standard emission-line diagnostic diagrams consistent with low-metallicity star-forming systems. Although the strong-line metallicity diagnostic R3 appears to decrease with increasing EW, we find no compelling evidence for a strong monotonic relation between EW and gas-phase metallicity when metallicities are inferred through full emission-line fitting. However, galaxies with stronger Ly$\alpha$ emission tend to lie below the average mass-metallicity relation at fixed stellar masses, suggesting that they are preferentially less chemically evolved than typical galaxies of the same mass. We conclude that high-EW LAEs provide useful, though imperfect, analogs of the galaxies thought to drive cosmic reionization, and combining EW with stellar mass may provide a more effective route for identifying the most chemically primitive galaxies.

papers.title: A machine-learning-driven dataset of 144,111 polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon infrared spectra for interpreting aromatic infrared bands
papers.abstract: The interpretation of interstellar aromatic infrared bands (AIBs) relies on reference spectral libraries, but the chemical space covered by existing databases remains incomplete relative to the vast structural diversity of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) expected in the interstellar medium. We present a large-scale, high-throughput PAH infrared (IR) spectral database that complements existing reference libraries by providing significantly more continuous coverage of the PAH chemical space for small to medium-sized PAHs. We used a machine-learning double-harmonic (ML-DH) framework that integrates neural network force fields with electronic dipole models. This framework achieves quantum-chemical accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost. It has been validated against independent density functional theory calculations and benchmark spectral databases. The resulting dataset comprises 144,111 IR spectra for 48,037 closed-shell, even-carbon benzenoid PAH structures across neutral, cationic, and anionic charge states, complete with per-spectrum uncertainty estimates. The spectral library, optimized geometries, and model code are publicly available. They can be used to complement existing libraries for interpreting and modeling JWST AIB observations and those from future IR missions.

papers.title: An Energetic Consistency Test for Feedback-Driven Gas Loss in Milky Way Dwarf Satellites
papers.abstract: Dwarf spheroidal galaxies (dSphs) contain little detectable cold gas, but the relative roles of stellar feedback, reionization, and environmental effects in their gas loss remain uncertain. We apply an order-of-magnitude energy-budget test to nine Milky Way dwarf satellites using published color--magnitude-diagram star formation histories (SFHs), galaxy-level velocity dispersions, effective radii, and integrated $V$-band luminosities. For each galaxy and halo prescription, we define the energy-equivalence time $\tau_{\mathrm{E}}$, when a crossing exists, as the first elapsed time at which the cumulative effective energy from core-collapse supernovae equals the adopted gas binding energy. This quantity is an energetic diagnostic rather than a direct measurement of wind launch. Under the fiducial parameters, all nine galaxies reach the nominal threshold under the kinematic--size prescription K+B16, yet star formation often continues long after threshold crossing. We compare the corresponding lookback time $t_{\mathrm{E,lb}}$ with $t_{90,\mathrm{lb}}$, the lookback time at which 90\% of the total initial stellar mass had formed. Because both times are derived from the same cumulative SFH, their temporal proximity is interpreted descriptively rather than as independent evidence of feedback-driven quenching. Whether the threshold is reached depends on the adopted halo mass, radius, retained gas fraction, and supernova--gas coupling efficiency. These results distinguish the availability of sufficient cumulative feedback energy from the processes that determine the timing of quenching.

papers.title: Dark Matter Particle Explorer: Ten-Year On-Orbit Performance and Scientific Outcomes
papers.abstract: The Dark Matter Particle Explorer (DAMPE, also known as ``Wukong'') is the first scientific space mission within the framework of the Strategic Pioneer Program on Space Science of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. The main scientific objectives of DAMPE include indirect detection of dark matter, cosmic-ray physics, and high energy gamma-ray astronomy. Thanks to its large geometrical factor and thick imaging calorimeter, DAMPE could effectively detect cosmic-ray electrons (including positrons) and gamma-rays up to 10~TeV, and nuclei up to PeV. Since launched on 17 December 2015 into a Sun-synchronous orbit, DAMPE has been smoothly operating on orbit for more than ten years. Here we present an overview of instrument, on-orbit status, and highlight scientific results of DAMPE, including the measurements of the all-electron energy spectrum and the spectra of protons and other nuclei, and high energy gamma-ray line search.

papers.title: Formation of Trapped Surfaces for the Einstein-Euler System
papers.abstract: We prove the formation of trapped surfaces for the Einstein--Euler system in 3+1 dimensions beyond spherical symmetry. We consider smooth characteristic initial data in a short-pulse regime with rapid fluid injection. Starting from initial data containing no trapped surfaces, we obtain two sufficient criteria for trapped surface formation, corresponding to the shear and fluid contributions, respectively. In particular, for the fluid-driven criterion, we impose no positive lower bound on the shear flux. To handle the multiple propagation speeds associated with gravitational waves, sound waves, and fluid transport, our analysis combines three ingredients: a coercive fluid energy current whose null fluxes reflect the unequal velocity components, curvature renormalizations adapted to the matter terms, and weighted geometric estimates controlling derivatives in all spacetime directions. To ensure that fluid injection alone can lead to trapped surface formation, we use particle-number conservation in a designed spacetime region to control the focusing process and obtain the desired sphere-integrated fluxes.

papers.title: Displacement-noise-free gravitational-wave detector using quantum tomography of photon orbital angular momentum states
papers.abstract: Gravitational waves (GWs) induce quantum transitions between photon orbital-angular-momentum (OAM) states with amplitudes $\alpha_{\pm}$. Exploiting this effect, we present a displacement-noise-free detection framework that extracts GW information from the OAM Hilbert space. Parametrized quantum state tomography of the GW-induced OAM sidebands enables a single V-shaped detector to resolve all seven wave parameters: the frequency, propagation direction, two polarization amplitudes, and initial phase of each polarization. Direct detection of the sidebands yields a weak signal of approximately $10^{-15}\,\mathrm{W}$. We therefore introduce a stronger reference state $r |0>_{\mathrm{P}}$, with $r=0.01$, to enhance the detected signal. For an arm length of $L=4\,\mathrm{m}$, $N=160$ round trips, a paraxial parameter of $\gamma=0.1$, an incident light power of $P_{\mathrm{BS}}=10\,\mathrm{kW}$, a wavelength of $\lambda_{\mathrm{opt}}=1064\,\mathrm{nm}$, and GW amplitudes of $A=10^{-18}$, we estimate sideband transition amplitudes of $|\alpha_{\pm}|\sim10^{-10}$ and signal powers of order $1\,\mathrm{nW}$, scaling as $P_{\mathrm{BS}}\alpha_{\pm}\propto P_{\mathrm{BS}}ANL\gamma/\lambda_{\mathrm{opt}}$. The shot-noise-limited sensitivity floor is $S^{1/2}_n=1.6\times10^{-20}\,\mathrm{Hz}^{-1/2}$. Because the scheme measures OAM transition amplitudes rather than differential arm lengths, it is intrinsically free from displacement noise and provides a broadband probe of GWs, specifically bridging the $0.1$--$10\,\mathrm{Hz}$ mid-frequency gap.

papers.title: Testing the inelastic dark matter interpretation of the LZ event with heavy-element experiments
papers.abstract: We consider the inelastic dark matter interpretation of the recent 248 keV event observed by LZ and identify different experiments that could test it. Details of the underlying model and the ability of complementary experiments to test it depend significantly on the high-velocity tail of the dark matter distribution. We consider several example velocity distributions motivated by the impact of the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) in order to map out the effects of this dependence. For example, we illustrate the type of high-velocity tail that would make the thermal Higgsino viable despite stringent constraints from solar neutrinos: Reducing the flux of the tail relative to simulation results improves the Higgsino fit, while extending the tail to higher velocities at fluxes below current simulation resolution evades the solar neutrino bound. This motivates more detailed simulations at higher resolution to understand the tail better. Even if xenon experiments confirm the signal event, complementary experiments are still required to test whether the underlying model is inelastic dark matter and to break degeneracies in the measurement of dark matter parameters such as mass and mass splitting. Heavy-element paleodetectors could cover most of the parameter space relevant to the LZ event. Their use of different elements could determine the dark matter mass and splitting, while their unique sensitivity to the history of the dark matter distribution could test the signal's LMC origin. Luminous detection in large neutrino detectors with heavy-element supplements could directly test the inelastic nature of the signal and measure the mass splitting, while its sensitivity to the radiative decay rate could provide strong evidence for the Higgsino interpretation.

papers.title: Disentangling geometry & growth in cosmic neutrino mass constraints: a more physical split and diagnostic
papers.abstract:
Recent cosmological data hint at a neutrino mass sum below the minimum value allowed by the neutrino mass oscillation experiments, with a preference for the opposite of massive neutrinos ("negative" neutrino masses). Since massive neutrinos impact the expansion history of the Universe, which in turn modifies the growth of structure, we ask whether such a preference originates from the observed geometry or structure growth, and whether the two agree. In this paper, we introduce a more physical split of $\sum m_
u$ into parameters $\sum m_
u^{geo}$ and $\sum m_
u^{growth}$ based on their physical effects, with extension to negative values. We split the expansion rate at the Boltzmann-code level: $\sum m_
u^{geo}$ sets $H(z)$ for distance computation, and $\sum m_
u^{growth}$ sets $H(z)$ for perturbation evolution. Combining Planck primary CMB, Planck+ACT+SPT CMB lensing and DESI BAO data, we find similar sensitivity and "negative" preference from geometry and growth with $\sum m_
u^{geo} = -0.07\pm0.10$ eV (68% C.L.) and $\sum m_
u^{growth} = -0.13^{+0.10}_{-0.12}$ eV (68% C.L.). The difference of the two is a null test of the $\Lambda$CDM model, passed by current data at $0.4\sigma$ level. Forecasts on Advanced SO CMB and DESI DR3 BAO show that $0.058$ eV would be rejected at $3.0\sigma$ from the geometry channel alone, if the negative mean of $\sum m_
u^{geo} = -0.07$ eV persists. The two channels can also provide a powerful new diagnostic between possible origins of the neutrino mass tension. With future CMB and BAO data, our Fisher forecasts show that an incorrect dark energy model displaces $\sum m_
u^{geo}$ from $0.058$ eV by $3.1$-$4.2\sigma$ and $\sum m_
u^{growth}$ by $1.1$-$1.3\sigma$, while an underestimated reionization optical depth reverses the pattern, $2.7$-$3.6\sigma$ in $\sum m_
u^{growth}$ against at most $0.23\sigma$ in $\sum m_
u^{geo}$. (Abridged)

papers.title: JWST reveals a highly ionized nebula powered by an ultraluminous X-ray source with a massive black hole in the metal-poor galaxy Holmberg II
papers.abstract: Recent James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations have revealed fine-structure lines of ions with ionization potentials ${\gtrsim}50$\,eV, such as [Ne\,{\sc v}] and [O\,{\sc iv}], in nebular spectra of some low-metallicity galaxies, raising questions about the nature of the ionizing sources. Ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs) have been considered as potential contributors, but direct evidence linking individual ULXs to highly ionized nebulae is limited. Here we present JWST IFU spectroscopy of the nebula surrounding the template ULX Ho\,II\,X--1 in the low-metallicity galaxy Holmberg\,II, already known to emit He\,{\sc ii}\,$\lambda4686$ and [O\,{\sc iv}]\,25.89\,$\mu$m lines. We resolve the infrared nebula on spatial scales of ${\sim}15-25$\,pc and report the first detections of [Ne\,{\sc v}] and [Ne\,{\sc vi}] in this source. We find anisotropic ionizing conditions: emission from the highest-ionization species arises from compact regions offset from the ULX toward the previously detected radio knots, whereas lower-ionization species trace the wider nebula. The preferential alignment of the highest-ionization emission with the radio axis suggests anisotropic escape of the ionizing continuum and a physical connection with jet-ejection activity. Spectral lines across the nebula are narrow and consistent with the instrumental resolution, indicating kinematically quiescent gas and disfavoring shocks as the dominant ionization mechanism. Together, these results provide direct evidence linking an individual ULX to a highly ionized nebula in a low-metallicity galaxy. These JWST observations of Ho~II~X--1 show that an accreting black hole in a low-metallicity galaxy is responsible for the extreme ionization of the surrounding nebula on ${\sim}100$\,pc scales.

papers.title: Self Calibrated Galaxy Groups from the DESI DR1 Bright Galaxy Survey
papers.abstract: We present a galaxy group catalog built from Data Release 1 of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Bright Galaxy Survey, using the Self Calibrated Group Finder. The algorithm uses clustering data from the observed sample to calibrate the Group Finder's free parameters, rather than simulations. The catalog contains 2,229,741 galaxies from ~$2680$ deg$^2$ of sky with 3-pass coverage and $r$-band fluxes $\lt 19.5$. The catalog classifies all galaxies in the flux-limited sample as centrals or satellites and estimates host dark matter halo masses. We show the satellite fraction $f_{\rm sat}$, luminosity halo mass relation, stellar halo mass relation and halo occupation distributions (HODs) from the catalog. We find these non-parametric HODs can be fit by standard HOD models, with satellite power-law index $\alpha$ values around 0.75 for star-forming galaxies and around 1.1 for quiescent objects. In agreement with recent results, we find that the quenched fraction of central galaxies depends mostly on halo mass and is nearly independent of central galaxy stellar mass for galaxies more massive than $10^{10.3}$ $M_\odot h^{-1}$ and halos more massive than $10^{12.2}$ $M_\odot h^{-1}$. In an appendix, we introduce a new Hybrid Nearest Neighbor (HNN) technique to mitigate systematics from fiber incompleteness. HNN uses photometric redshifts and multiple on-sky neighbors to assign redshifts to unobserved targets. Calibrated on DESI Survey Validation 3 data, our technique yields correct redshifts $\sim 50\%$ of the time and produces unbiased halo occupation statistics.

papers.title: Study of pulse jitter characteristics of PSR J1744-1134: Towards high precision pulsar timing with InPTA
papers.abstract: Variations in the shapes of individual pulses introduce a broadband noise component in pulsar times of arrival beyond what is expected from radiometer noise, referred to as the jitter noise. This noise limits the timing accuracy and, consequently, the sensitivity required for the detection of nanohertz gravitational waves using pulsar timing arrays. Accurate characterization of jitter noise, including its amplitude and frequency dependence, is therefore essential for each pulsar. In this work, we present the first detailed study of jitter noise in PSR J1744-1134 over the frequency range 300-500 MHz, using observations from the Indian Pulsar Timing Array experiment conducted with the upgraded Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope. We detect clear signatures of jitter in this pulsar through pulse-level analysis and Bayesian inference. Furthermore, we investigated the frequency dependence of the jitter noise and compared our results with earlier measurements at higher frequencies. The observed differences in jitter amplitude suggest a possible frequency evolution, highlighting the importance of low-frequency studies for improving pulsar timing precision and accuracy. We also investigated the effect of jitter on the high precision dispersion measure derived from our observations and found that jitter is not the limiting factor for DM precision achieved for this pulsar in the given observation timescale.

papers.title: Correlated Radio Frequency Interference Monitor for Radio Telescopes
papers.abstract: Radio frequency interference (RFI) is one of the biggest challenges facing current radio astronomy experiments. Telescopes like the Canadian Hydrogen Observatory and Radio transient Detector (CHORD) need to accurately identify RFI to deliver on their science goals. For applications like HI intensity mapping for precision cosmology, long integrations consisting of hundreds to thousands of hours are needed, and thorough RFI flagging is required to avoid contaminating deep datasets. Currently, many major precision cosmology instruments are facing systematic limitations that include unflagged RFI contamination. For transients, false triggers due to RFI are common and interfere with the detection of real sources like fast radio bursts (FRBs). This paper presents a prototype design for an auxiliary array of horizon-pointed antennas that are cross-correlated in real-time at full cadence with the main telescope to assist in the identification and mitigation of RFI for the CHORD instrument. The major benefit of the version proposed here over a more traditional omnidirectional observatory monitor is the capability to synchronize with CHORD in real time and provide fine timescale flags and cross correlations. The general setup and techniques used here will be applicable to other radio telescopes as well.

papers.title: Ergodic topology sampling toward the continuum with Stochastic Normalizing Flows
papers.abstract: In this work we provide numerical evidence that topological freezing in $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ Yang-Mills theory can be mitigated with a flow-based approach, as tested at lattice spacings as fine as 0.03~fm. We do so by analyzing the scaling of the costs of a computational strategy based on the combination of open boundary conditions and Stochastic Normalizing Flows. We show that the integrated autocorrelation time of the squared topological charge and the statistical uncertainty on the topological susceptibility remain under control throughout the explored parameter range with currently available computational resources. This marks an important step toward the use of even more efficient flow-based architectures for ergodic sampling of topology in state-of-the-art lattice gauge theory calculations.

papers.title: Multi-Method Machine Learning Classification of Astronomical Sources with Rubin Data Previews: a Spectroscopy-Free Approach with DP1 and DP2
papers.abstract: We present a multi-method machine-learning study for the binary photometric classification of point-like and extended sources in the Rubin Observatory Data Preview 1 (DP1) and Data Preview 2 (DP2). The workflow runs on the Rubin Science Platform using DP1 and DP2 ugrizy photometry, the DP1 ancillary photometric-redshift catalog, and the Monster astrometric and photometric reference catalog, without relying on external spectroscopy. Six methods (SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost, k-Nearest Neighbors, an Artificial Neural Network, and a soft Voting ensemble) are benchmarked in the deepest DP1 field, the Extended Chandra Deep Field South. These methods reach 10-fold cross-validation macro-F1 scores of 0.95-0.97 on the balanced training subset and test macro-F1 scores of 0.87-0.92 on the imbalanced held-out set, with RF and the SV ensemble tied at the top (0.918); the differences among the leading methods are within the statistical uncertainty. Permutation importance identifies FWHM as the dominant feature, and the six methods agree on 79.5% of the full catalog. The same pipeline is then applied without retuning the settings to the two other DP1 fields with full ugrizy coverage and photometric-redshift support, Euclid Deep Field South and the Low Galactic Latitude Field. Together, the three fields span a factor of approximately 7 in E(B-V) and approximately 10 in stellar density, yet headline macro-F1 remains above 0.87 in every field. We then apply the same pipeline to four DP2 fields (ECDFS, COSMOS, EDFS, and ELAIS-S1). Using colors and morphology, the best method reaches a test macro-F1 of 0.83 to 0.88 across these fields, and the six methods agree on 77 to 86% of each catalog. Adding the per-band photometric uncertainties as features raises the best macro-F1 to about 0.95 in ECDFS DP1 and 0.97 in ECDFS DP2 (and to approximately 0.97-0.98 in the other fields).

papers.title: The dawn of the first galaxies
papers.abstract: Understanding how the first galaxies assembled their stellar mass at cosmic dawn is a central frontier of modern astrophysics. JWST has now revealed an unexpected population of ultraviolet-bright galaxies at z>10, whose intense emission points towards a rapid stellar mass growth that challenges current models of early galaxy assembly. Yet, the cold gas fueling this growth remains hidden: current ALMA sensitivity restricts routine detection to only the brightest ionized-gas tracers such as [OIII] 88$\mu$m, while [CII] 158$\mu$m, a key coolant and gas-mass proxy of the neutral interstellar medium (ISM), is undetected beyond $z\sim8$. This leaves fundamental questions unanswered: how quickly primeval galaxies gathered cold gas and turned it into stars; what physical conditions (density, temperature, radiation field) characterized their ISM; how fast metals and dust built up; and how feedback regulated early gas assembly. Only a transformational sub-millimeter facility like ALMA2040 can address these questions, enabling systematic surveys of [CII] in the first galaxies and providing a representative census of gas fractions and depletion times. A simulated galaxy at $z=11.3$ shows that ALMA2040 not only will detect, but also spatially resolve its merging cold-gas structure in [CII] on $\sim$200 pc scales in 5 hours (below 100 pc in 10 hours). ALMA2040 will also spectrally resolve multiple lines simultaneously, akin to integral-field spectroscopy, providing the key diagnostics needed to break density-metallicity-radiation-field degeneracies and map the multi-phase ISM of z>10 galaxies. The combination of dramatically increased line sensitivity and wide instantaneous bandwidth will push the search for the first galaxies out to the earliest cosmic times, with [OIII] detectable up to $z\sim20$. ALMA2040 will thus be transformative for understanding how the first galaxies assembled at cosmic dawn.

papers.title: Compact Dark Matter with Globular Cluster Pulsars
papers.abstract: Pulsars are exceptionally stable clocks, and a compact dark-matter object passing near the line of sight to a pulsar delays its pulses through the Shapiro effect. The number of detectable transits is set by the integral over the dark-matter density along the line of sight connecting the Earth and the pulsar. Established pulsars in pulsar timing arrays are typically within one kiloparsec of the Earth and hence sit in a dark-matter density comparable to our local value. In this work, we explore globular clusters in the inner Galaxy as targets to search for compact dark matter. These high-pulsar-density environments can be cheaply observed with a single telescope beam and enjoy a large dark-matter crossing rate. Additionally, since the recently detected nanohertz gravitational-wave background is nearly common to the cluster's pulsars, a multi-pulsar analysis can remove much of its contribution. Ranking known clusters, we find that Terzan 5, with 49 pulsars, offers the best reach. A forty-year campaign of weekly four-hour visits at the sensitivity envisioned for the second phase of the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) would probe compact objects making up $6\%$ of the dark matter at $0.02\,M_\odot$. Finally, we estimate the foreground from stars and stellar remnants in Terzan 5 and along the sightline. It is subdominant near the most sensitive low-mass part of the SKA benchmark, but becomes important over parts of the stellar mass range.

papers.title: ALMA2040: Understanding the Early Assembly of Galaxies - The Formation of Star-Forming Clumps and their Role in Shaping Galaxy Evolution
papers.abstract: Astrophysics seeks to explain how galaxies form and evolve through the interplay of stars, gas, and dust. Giant molecular clouds (GMCs), the main reservoirs and sites of star formation, link the cold interstellar medium to the birth of stars and stellar structures. Their properties reflect galactic disk conditions, and their evolution is shaped by stellar feedback and host-galaxy dynamics. Studying GMCs across cosmic time is therefore key to understanding how gas turns into stars and drives galaxy evolution. Hubble Space Telescope and James Webb Space Telescope observations reveal compact star-forming clumps in galaxies from Cosmic Noon to the Epoch of Reionization ($z\approx6$), but their link to the molecular gas reservoir is still unclear. We do not yet know how GMC properties vary with redshift and environment, how molecular gas, dust, and young stars are arranged, or whether clumps form in unstable disks or disturbed systems. Addressing these questions requires spatially resolved observations of the cold interstellar medium at the scales probed by optical/near-infrared facilities. ALMA2040, a transformational next-generation sub-mm facility, will provide the sensitivity and angular resolution needed to detect individual GMCs in representative lensed and unlensed galaxies at $z>1$. CO and [CII], complemented by dust continuum and molecular-gas kinematics, will measure the molecular gas reservoir, its physical conditions, and its dynamical state. Together with JWST and the ELT, ALMA2040 will connect cold gas, dust, and stellar structures across cosmic time. ALMA2040 will revolutionize our understanding of (i) the properties and evolution of GMCs and their connection to star-forming clumps, (ii) the spatial interplay between molecular gas, dust, and young stars, and (iii) the dynamics, survival, and formation of GMCs and stellar clumps.

papers.title: Has JWST Seen Everything? Hunting for "NIRCam-dark" Dusty Star-Forming Galaxies at $z 6 - 9$ with ALMA2040
papers.abstract: JWST/NIRCam has recovered the stellar counterparts of many ALMA-detected, formerly HST-dark galaxies, yet ALMA has started identifying dusty star-forming galaxies (DSFGs) at $z>6$ that remain extremely faint or undetected even with NIRCam. These "NIRCam-dark" DSFGs may trace a missing rapid-growth phase connecting UV-luminous galaxies at $z>10$ to massive quiescent galaxies at $z\gtrsim4$. So far, the small, heterogeneously selected NIRCam-dark sample is insufficient to determine their abundance or role in the evolution of massive galaxies. We show that a blind 1.3-mm continuum survey with ALMA2040 can provide the first high-significance census of this elusive NIRCam-dark DSFG population across $z\simeq 6 - 9$. We conduct sensitivity and survey-speed calculations requiring a $10\sigma$ detection of a NIRCam-dark DSFG with a dust-obscured star-formation rate of $60\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$ at $z = 8$. At a like-for-like 7.5-GHz normalization, ALMA2040 will reach the required 1.3-mm RMS of $21\,\mu$Jy beam$^{-1}$ about 90 times faster than current ALMA. With 100 hr on-source, ALMA2040 can cover an area of $\sim0.5$ deg$^2$ and detect $\langle N \rangle\sim16$ NIRCam-dark DSFGs over $7.5<9$, assuming a fiducial number density $n=3\times10^{-6}$ cMpc$^{-3}$. Dividing the survey among independent fields with deep JWST coverage would mitigate cosmic variance and enable immediate NIRCam, MIRI, and spectroscopic characterization of their environments. The $\geq512$-GHz instantaneous bandwidth expected for ALMA2040 will also detect [C II] line at a wide redshift range, supplementing the continuum discovery with redshift confirmation. Such a survey will test whether NIRCam-dark DSFGs trace a missing rapid-growth phase between the earliest UV-luminous galaxies at $z>10$ and the rapid emergence of massive quiescent systems at $z\gtrsim 4$.

papers.title: An Attenuation Bump at z=9.3: Probing Dust Diversity at Cosmic Dawn
papers.abstract: We report the identification of a UV attenuation bump in the Black Pearl, a galaxy at a spectroscopic redshift of 9.3335 observed with JWST/NIRSpec as part of the ZENITH and EMBER surveys. This is the highest-redshift UV bump reported to date, probing dust properties only approximately 500 Myr after the Big Bang. The feature is directly detected as a broad depression in the rest-frame UV continuum and is well described by a local Drude profile, with a central wavelength of 2132+/-17 Angstroms, an FWHM of 413+/-54 Angstroms, and a peak attenuation of 0.21+/-0.02 mag. Joint spectrophotometric modeling with a flexible attenuation law independently recovers a pronounced UV bump without imposing its presence a priori, regardless of the adopted star-formation history. The modeling indicates a relatively low-mass, actively star-forming galaxy, with a logarithmic stellar mass of 8.35 (+0.09/-0.08) in solar units, a star-formation rate of 2.36 (+0.54/-0.42) solar masses per year, and a visual attenuation of 0.34 (+0.12/-0.11) mag. Rest-frame optical emission-line diagnostics indicate a hard ionizing spectrum and allow for a moderate AGN contribution, but provide no evidence for a powerful AGN capable of dominating the observed UV continuum. The bump is blueshifted by 43+/-17 Angstroms (approximately 2.5 sigma) relative to the canonical Milky Way 2175 Angstrom feature and by 127 +/- 17 Angstroms relative to the few UV bumps currently known at redshift approximately 7, while its width is consistent with the broad distribution measured along Milky Way sightlines. The displaced central wavelength therefore provides the clearest evidence for a nonstandard UV-bump profile at redshift 9.3335, pointing to substantial diversity in the properties of UV-bump carriers at early cosmic times, with both PAHs and small graphite grains remaining plausible candidates.

papers.title: Nonlocal Gravity, Restricted CPL Dynamics and DESI Constraints
papers.abstract: Nonlocal modifications of gravity provide a theoretically motivated framework in which cosmic acceleration can emerge dynamically without introducing a fundamental cosmological constant. We revisit the cosmological predictions of the Maggiore--Mancarella nonlocal $R\,\Box^{-2}R$ model, with particular emphasis on its background dynamics and observational viability in light of recent DESI baryon acoustic oscillation measurements. A key feature of the theory is its predictive character: for fixed standard cosmological parameters, each value of the nonlocal parameter determines a specific effective pair $(w_0,w_a)$, so that the model traces a restricted trajectory in the Chevallier--Polarski--Linder plane rather than spanning the full phenomenological parameter space. We construct this mapping explicitly and confront the model with observations by implementing its cosmological dynamics in a Boltzmann solver and performing a Markov chain Monte Carlo analysis using Cosmic Microwave Background, supernova, and DESI BAO data. We find that current datasets constrain the nonlocal parameter close to the $\Lambda$CDM limit, with no statistically significant preference for nonlocal deviations.

papers.title: Wandering intermediate-mass black holes and off-nuclear tidal disruption events from early star clusters
papers.abstract: Off-nuclear tidal disruption events (TDEs) reveal evidence for massive black holes outside galactic centers, but the origins of this wandering population remain uncertain. We investigate wandering intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) formed through runaway stellar collisions in dense, high-redshift star clusters and predict their TDE signatures across cosmic time. Our semi-analytic model samples clusters associated with low-mass subhalos at $7<20$ and uses merger trees from the IllustrisTNG TNG50 simulation to follow the assembly of 15 elliptical galaxies with stellar masses of $10^9-10^{11}~M_\odot$. We compare two models for high-redshift cluster formation: a maximal model taken from a high-resolution simulation and a conservative model calibrated from local cluster relations. Off-nuclear TDEs produced through this mechanism occur in bursts within 10-100 Myr of IMBH formation as the loss-cone surrounding the black hole is depleted. We estimate the rate of off-nuclear TDEs expected across time per galaxy, and characterize these events as typically occurring between $10-10^3$ kpc from their host galaxy centers. Event rates increase with galaxy mass; in the maximal model, the progenitors of the most massive galaxies reach peak off-nuclear TDE rates of approximately $5\times10^{-4}-4\times10^{-2}~\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ per galaxy at $7\lesssim z\lesssim13$. This work provides a framework for constraining the early population of star clusters that form IMBHs through runaway collapse via their contribution to the rate of off-nuclear TDEs in the high redshift Universe.

papers.title: HI rotation curves and mass-size relation for 568 galaxies from the Apertif Wide-area Extragalactic Survey
papers.abstract: The extended HI rotation curves of galaxies are one of the most powerful tools for studying galaxy evolution and for testing different dark matter and modified gravity models. However, their sample sizes have historically been limited to a few hundred galaxies, mostly due to the survey speed of radio interferometers. Here, we present a first data release of HI kinematic models from the Apertif Wide-area Extragalactic Survey (AWES). Starting from 1924 galaxies detected in HI, we constructed 568 reliable kinematic models, which provide rotation curves, velocity dispersion profiles, surface density profiles, and HI disk geometries. This dataset constitutes the largest homogeneous HI rotation curve sample to date. The HI disks of the modeled galaxies span three orders of magnitude in HI mass, have outer rotation velocities between ~20 and ~300 km/s, and extend from 2 to more than 60 kpc. The number of data points of the rotation curves ranges from 3 to 23, with a peak value at 4 and a broad tail to larger values. The rotation curves display a variety of inner shapes, but in general, they tend to become flat at large radii. Based on the HI surface density profiles derived during the kinematic modeling, we studied the HI mass-size relation with a large homogeneous sample of 213 galaxies. The relation is very tight, with an observed scatter along the mass direction of ~0.101 dex and an inferred intrinsic scatter along the same direction of only 0.067 +/- 0.007 dex. The best fitting slope is 1.96 +/- 0.03 when fitting for mass as a function of size, indicating that HI disks have a constant average surface density.

papers.title: The unified Bound Dark Energy--Bound Dark Matter model: theory and constraints from DESI DR2
papers.abstract: The unified Bound Dark Energy--Bound Dark Matter (BDE-BDM) model derives both the dark energy and the whole of the dark matter from a single supersymmetric $SU(3)$ gauge group with $N_f=6$ flavors. Gauge-coupling unification predicts the scale at which it condenses, $\Lc=34^{+16}_{-11}$~eV, before any cosmological data are used, so the dark-energy sector adds no parameter to those of \LCDM\ and the dark-matter sector adds only one. Fitting DESI DR2 BAO, Planck CMB, Planck+ACT DR6 CMB lensing, and three supernova compilations (PantheonPlus, Union3.1, DES-Dovekie) gives, for Union3.1, $\Lc=43.67\pm0.13$~eV, inside the predicted range: a high-energy prediction met by a late-time measurement. The equation of state evolves to $w_0=-0.9262\pm0.0005$ and never crosses the phantom divide. Relative to \LCDM\ the model lowers the DESI BAO $\chi^2$ by $2.95$--$3.67$ and the supernova $\chi^2$ by $2.53$--$4.07$, recovering $57\%$--$71\%$ of the total reduction that \wowa\ obtains by fitting two dark-energy parameters to the same data, and reaching the lower BAO $\chi^2$ of the two models for two of the three compilations. Its $\Delta\mathrm{DIC}$ against \LCDM\ is strong for every compilation, $-8.28$ to $-7.47$, varying by $0.81$ where that of \wowa\ varies by $4.8$. Because the dark-energy sector adds no parameter to those of \LCDM, the likelihood gain survives the Occam penalty: $\ln B=+4.09$, $+4.12$, and $+4.83$ against \LCDM, where \wowa\ gives $-2.11$, $-0.26$, and $-0.56$. Among six models pairing a cosmological constant, the \wowa\ parametrization or bound dark energy with cold or bound dark matter, BDE-BDM has the largest Bayesian evidence.

papers.title: The Pristine survey XXIX. Data Release 2: Photometric metallicities for 15 millions stars down to $G 20.5$
papers.abstract: Tailored narrow-band photometric observations are an efficient way to measure the metallicity of Milky Way stars. The Pristine survey has been mapping the northern sky since 2015 using narrow-band $CaHK$ photometry obtained with the MegaCam imager on the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope (CFHT). Data Release 1 (DR1) provided a high-precision absolute calibration of the survey observed before October 2022 using \Gaia DR3 XP synthetic photometry, yielding photometric metallicities over $\sim$6,500 deg$^2$, but was limited in depth to the availability of \Gaia spectro-photometry ($G \lesssim 17.65$). We present the Pristine Data Release 2 (DR2) that includes all Pristine observations until January 2025, corresponding to an additional 1,500\,deg$^2$ of coverage, and including all faint sources down to $G\sim20.5$. This release aims to exploit the full depth of the Pristine observations to uncover the faint metal-poor halo. We process all images observed from the start of the survey in March 2015 through to January 2025 following the methodology presented in DR1. The core of the calibration utilizes the subset of bright stars with \Gaia synthetic $CaHK_\mathrm{syn}$ magnitudes to train the \texttt{PhotCalib} neural network. We then derive photometric metallicities using the established Pristine ($CaHK, G, G_{\rm BP}, G_{\rm RP}$) to [Fe/H] model. The resulting catalogue covers approximately $\sim$ 8,000 deg$^{2}$ and provides photometric metallicities for 15 millions FGK stars, which show good agreement with recently published, independent Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) metallicities. With its increased coverage and access to a significantly fainter regime compared to DR1, DR2 significantly increases the volume of the survey. We report more than 200,000 and 6,500 very and extremely metal-poor star candidates, respectively.

papers.title: Probing ordered magnetic fields in galaxies across cosmic time
papers.abstract: Magnetic fields are dynamically important across many astronomical environments, yet their origin, strength, and evolution over cosmic time remain poorly understood. Ordered magnetic fields are ubiquitous in the nearby Universe, as revealed by a range of observational techniques, but evidence for their existence at cosmological distances is scarce. Recent ALMA detections of polarised dust emission indicate that galactic-scale ordered magnetic fields, spanning up to kiloparsec scales, were already present in massive star-forming galaxies at redshifts up to $z\sim5.6$. This white paper argues that the ALMA2040 concept -- with its nearly tenfold improvement in sensitivity and angular resolution, and full-polarisation capability extended to higher-frequency bands -- will open up the study of cosmic magnetism in the early Universe. We identify four science drivers: constraining the dynamos that generate galactic-scale ordered fields, measuring the strength of early magnetic fields, connecting magnetic fields to galaxy evolution across cosmic time, and constraining dust grain properties through the polarised spectral energy distribution. We summarise the corresponding requirements in angular resolution, spectral coverage, and sensitivity, and discuss synergies with next-generation telescopes.

papers.title: Tracing small-scale structure formation through cosmic time with strong gravitational lensing: A case for a next-generation sub-millimetre/millimetre interferometer
papers.abstract: The nature of dark matter and the growth of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) remain major open questions in modern astrophysics. Both leave a key signature in an overlapping, largely unexplored mass range: $<10^7$ M$_{\odot}$ dark haloes and wandering black holes. These may be undetectable directly, but detectable through gravitational perturbation of strongly lensed images, and partly or entirely distinguishable from one another through lensing data alone. We demonstrate through realistic simulations that a 255-element sub-mm/mm interferometer could probe this critical mass regime, detecting gravitational perturbations in strongly lensed dusty star-forming galaxies (DSFGs) from objects down to at least $10^5$ M$_{\odot}$. Combined with lens-galaxy characterisation from the European Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), which strengthens the physical interpretation of detected perturbers, and the unprecedented lens samples expected from Euclid and the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), this facility could deliver a census of low-mass dark matter haloes and wandering massive black holes across cosmic time.

papers.title: How Little Red Dots Turn Blue: Evolution of Kelvin-Helmholtz Contracting Black Hole Envelopes and Observational Diagnostics
papers.abstract: James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations have revealed compact, red-colored, broad-line emitters known as little red dots (LRDs), while a bluer counterpart population has been referred to as little blue dots (LBDs). Their physical connection remains unclear: they may represent different evolutionary stages of the same phenomenon, distinct populations, or different phases of the broader evolution of early galaxies and their black holes (BHs). We propose a model in which a rapidly growing BH is embedded in a geometrically thick gaseous envelope accompanied by concurrent nuclear star formation. The model reproduces the observed spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of LRDs and LBDs, and naturally connects the two phases through Kelvin-Helmholtz contraction of the envelope and exposure of the nuclear accretion disk, as the gas supply declines due to external stellar activity or feedback. We predict the corresponding evolutionary tracks in the UV-optical slope ($\beta_{\rm UV}$-$\beta_{\rm opt}$) plane which bridge the apparent gap between LRDs and LBDs. These evolutionary tracks start from the LRD regime and consistently exhibit a red excursion that extends toward $(\beta_{\rm UV},\beta_{\rm opt})\sim(2,-1)$ before turning toward the LBD regime. This feature is largely insensitive to variations in the model parameters that govern the envelope structure, providing a robust signature of the transitional population. The transition lasts $\sim5$-$50\,\mathrm{Myr}$, depending primarily on the BH feedback efficiency and the gas-retention efficiency of the envelope. The abundance ratio of transitional systems to LRDs therefore provides a constraint on BH feedback and gas retention during the rapid growth of early supermassive BHs.

papers.title: Technically Natural Baryogenesis with the QCD Axion
papers.abstract: The strong CP problem, dark matter, and the observed baryon abundance may all be connected dynamically through the QCD axion, though whether this connection is realized in Nature depends on additional degrees of freedom. We show that the required dynamics can arise from technically natural ingredients if multiple axions mix through the QCD anomaly. We review the connection between axion rotation and the baryon asymmetry, revisit the axiogenesis and kinetic-misalignment proposals, and derive new limits on their dynamics. Motivated by these considerations, naturalness and axion quality, we construct a realization in which mixing with additional axions both enhances the effective QCD axion field range through monodromy and dissipates excess rotational energy through mixing with a dark confining gauge sector, thereby avoiding overclosure. We study the resulting effective dynamics in several illustrative limits, uncovering phenomena that may arise more generally in multi-axion theories. We numerically evolve the full coupled system and show that it can simultaneously reproduce the observed baryon asymmetry and dark matter abundance within a predictive region of parameter space testable by near-future direct and indirect searches. Depending on the model parameters, either the QCD axion or the new heavy axion constitutes the dominant dark matter component. Successful baryogenesis favors a QCD axion decay constant near its current astrophysical lower bound, while the heavy axion lies within reach of forthcoming astrophysical and cosmological observations.

papers.title: CoRGI in MaNGA - II. NGC 5717: cold-gas accretion and disk growth in a BGG
papers.abstract: Large-scale stellar counter-rotation, in which two coplanar stellar components rotate in opposite directions, is usually interpreted as a signature of external gas accretion. Such systems are most often found in relatively sparse environments, where cold gas can be acquired and remain dynamically undisturbed long enough to settle into a disk. It is less clear whether this channel can operate in massive central galaxies, whose group or cluster environments can heat, strip, or perturb cold gas. Here we present NGC 5717, one of the most massive galaxies known to host a counter-rotating stellar disk and the first identified case in a brightest group galaxy. Using integral-field spectroscopy from SDSS-IV Mapping Nearby Galaxies at Apache Point Observatory (MaNGA), together with CFHT imaging, ancillary HI data, and SDSS/DESI spectroscopy of the surrounding group, we show that the galaxy contains a dynamically cold counter-rotating disk embedded in an old dynamically hot elliptical component. The disk is young ($\sim 1.3$ Gyr), metal-poor ([Fe/H] $\sim -0.7$ dex), extended ($h \sim 2.4$ kpc), and massive ($\log M_\star/M_\odot \sim 9.9$); the associated ionized gas co-rotates with it, while the available HI data indicate no significant remaining reservoir of neutral atomic gas ($\log M_{\mathrm{HI}}/M_\odot \lesssim 9$). These properties support an in situ origin of the secondary component from externally accreted gas. The chemical evolution model favors gas accretion from a cosmic filament, which is consistent with the surrounding cosmic-web geometry, and indicates highly efficient burst-like star formation with substantial metal-enriched outflows. NGC 5717 may therefore represent a rare example of disk growth in a massive central galaxy, enabled by external cold-gas accretion during an earlier phase of the group assembly history.

papers.title: Efficient numerical evolution of self-gravitating systems with dark-matter-baryon scattering
papers.abstract: We present a fast algorithm to numerically evolve a spherically symmetric system consisting of dark matter and gas, including dark-matter-baryon scattering. The method augments the spherical N-body code NSphere, which collapses the six-dimensional phase space of a spherical collisionless system to three dimensions, with a one-dimensional Lagrangian treatment of gas. Dark-matter-baryon scattering is implemented as a Monte-Carlo process between the dark-matter numerical particles and the gas shells. We also implement an algorithm for radiative gas cooling that is valid for weak cooling. The gas, as well as dark-matter-baryon scattering and cooling, adds only incrementally to the run time of the code, allowing systems to be evolved on a laptop computer, a tiny fraction of the computational resources required for a full 3D N-body/hydro simulation. To illustrate, we show the evolution of a $\sim 10^{13}\,M_\odot$ halo with a dark-matter-baryon scattering cross section $\sigma_{\rm tot}/m_\chi=0.1\,{\rm cm}^2\,{\rm g}^{-1}$ but no gas cooling. We then show examples with radiative gas cooling where the cooling is altered through interaction with dark-matter particles. The resulting code, NSphere-IDM, allows the implications of dark-matter interactions for galaxy evolution to be explored quickly over large volumes of the dark-matter parameter space, and other new physics (e.g., dark-matter self-interactions or anisotropy in the distribution function) is easily incorporated. The code can also provide useful calibrations and benchmarks for fully 3D N-body or hydrodynamical simulations.

papers.title: A Misaligned Debris Disk relative to the Host Star CPD-72 2713 from JWST/NIRCam Imaging
papers.abstract: Observations of debris disks provide a valuable window to investigate the formation and evolution of planetary systems. We present high-contrast JWST/NIRCam observations of CPD-72 2713, a 24 Myr-old star that belongs to the $\beta$ Pic moving group. We obtained the first scattered-light images of the disk in both F210M and F444W filters, revealing a nearly face-on orientation. Forward modeling yields disk radii of $\rm 55.4^{+3.0}_{-3.2}\,AU$ (F210M) and $\rm 39.1^{+4.6}_ {-2.6}\,AU$ (F444W), both significantly smaller than the thermal emission radii measured with ALMA and Herschel/PACS. This discrepancy suggests that scattered light traces the inner region of the disk while thermal emission probes the outer regions. Combining the stellar rotation period ($4.47\pm0.67$ days) from TESS light curves and spectroscopic $v\sin i_*$, we constrained the stellar inclination to $47^{\circ}.2^{+11.1}_{-7.7}$ ($1\sigma$). The minimum star-disk mutual inclinations are $27^{\circ}.6 _{-8.2} ^{+11.5}\ (1\sigma)$ from F210M data and $27^{\circ}.3 _{-10.9}^{ +12.5}\ (1\sigma)$ in F444W data. We find that the minimum star--disk mutual inclination exceeds $10^\circ$ at the $95\%$ credible level in both F210M and F444W, suggesting a misalignment between the scattered-light disk and the stellar equatorial plane. We note that variation among published disk inclination measurements and potential systematic uncertainties may affect this probability. With JWST high-contrast imaging, we rule out planets down to $0.3\ \rm M_{J}$ at $0.5^{\prime\prime}$ and beyond, disfavoring a planet as the driver of the star-disk misalignment.

papers.title: A Vision for Little Red Dots in the Low-Redshift Universe with ALMA2040
papers.abstract: The discovery of Little Red Dots (LRDs) at high redshifts with JWST has revealed a previously unknown phase of black-hole growth. However, their black-hole (BH) masses, BH-to-stellar mass ratios, cold-gas reservoirs, and depletion times remain uncertain. The recent discovery of low-redshift LRDs at $z\simeq0.1 - 0.9$ creates a decisive opportunity to access their low-$J$ CO lines for measuring molecular gas reservoirs, and the nearest systems can in principle be spatially resolved. We use J1025+1402 ("The Egg") at $z=0.1007$, the best-studied local LRD, as a benchmark to explore the scientific opportunities with ALMA2040. Assuming a molecular gas mass of $10^9\,M_\odot$, the CO(2-1) detectability strongly depends on the assumed CO-to-H$_2$ conversion ($\alpha_{\rm CO}$). With a large $\alpha_{\rm CO} \simeq 315 - 725\,M_\odot\,({\rm K\,km\,s}^{-1}\,{\rm pc}^2)^{-1}$ at a low gas-phase metallicity, the CO line would remain very challenging for the current ALMA to detect, while ALMA2040 will likely deliver a robust CO detection and thus a gas-reservoir constraint for The Egg. Furthermore, with the best angular resolution at its CO(2-1) frequency (14.6 mas, or 27 pc), ALMA2040 may spatially resolve the CO emission from The Egg. Assuming an optimistic, SMC-like $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ with a 50-hour deep integration, we produce mock position-velocity diagrams that may distinguish a $10^7\,M_\odot$ black hole from the no-BH model through its steeper central velocity structure. We conclude that ALMA2040 has the potential to directly measure the gas masses, depletion times, and excitation of local LRDs, while the CO-bright subset may ultimately yield dynamical constraints on the mass of their central black holes.

papers.title: JWST Observations of RR Lyrae in Leo P
papers.abstract: We analyze co-spatial HST/ACS and JWST/NIRCam time-series photometric observations of RR Lyrae in the low-metallicity dwarf galaxy Leo P. This study provides a new opportunity to explore the properties of and potential for metal-poor RR Lyrae studies with JWST using well-understood relationships from past HST work. We identify 20 RR Lyrae in the HST imaging and 15 RR Lyrae in the JWST imaging. We determine the periods, amplitudes, and mean magnitudes for each of the RR Lyrae. We fit the Period-Wesenheit-Metallicity (PWZ) function to the HST RR Lyrae population, and obtain a Gaia-consistent RR Lyrae-based distance to Leo P of $\mu = 26.04\pm0.07$ ($1.61\pm0.06$ Mpc), consistent with existing distance measurements. We determine a JWST-based PWZ using Leo P data along with previous JWST RR Lyrae observations in WLM. The simultaneous fit decreases the mean fractional uncertainty by 31% on the slope and by 11% on the intercept, increasing the constraining power as compared to the existing calibration.
